title: Object literals, property keys, and descriptors
hook: Almost every JavaScript value you pass around — config objects, API payloads, event handlers — starts as an object literal. Before prototypes and classes make sense, you need to know how keys, values, and hidden descriptor flags actually behave at runtime.

blocks.text: An **object literal** is the `{ key: value }` syntax for creating a plain object. Keys are usually strings or **Symbols**; values can be any JavaScript value including functions (called **methods** when defined inside the literal). Every property also has a hidden **descriptor** — three flags (`writable`, `enumerable`, `configurable`) that control whether you can change, list, or delete it.

entries.plainDefinition: Syntax `{ a: 1, b: 2 }` that creates a new plain object in one expression.
Metadata on a property: writable (can assign?), enumerable (shows in for-in?), configurable (can delete/redefine?).
A key computed at runtime using square brackets in the literal.
When the key name matches a variable name, you can write `{ name }` instead of `{ name: name }`.

blocks.text: Object literals are the building block for configuration, Data Transfer Objects (DTOs), and module exports. In TypeScript, structural typing means two interfaces with the same shape assign freely — but at runtime they are just plain objects with no type name attached. Property descriptors matter when you freeze API surfaces (`Object.freeze`), hide internal fields from `JSON.stringify`, or debug why `for...in` lists some keys and not others.

blocks.title: Literals create own properties
blocks.body: Keys you write in `{ a: 1 }` become **own** properties on the new object. They are not inherited from `Object.prototype` unless you explicitly put them on the prototype — that distinction drives the prototype chain topic next.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Engine creates a new object
items.body: The runtime allocates an object whose internal [[Prototype]] is `Object.prototype` (unless you use `Object.create(null)`).

items.title: Each key becomes an own property
items.body: String keys are coerced (`123` becomes `"123"`). Symbol keys stay as Symbols and never collide with string keys.

items.title: Default descriptor flags apply
items.body: Data properties from literals default to `writable: true`, `enumerable: true`, `configurable: true` — unless you use `Object.defineProperty` or class fields with different rules.

items.title: Methods are just function-valued properties
items.body: `{ greet() {} }` is shorthand for `{ greet: function() {} }`. The function's `this` depends on how it is called — not on the literal syntax.

diagram.title: Object literal structure
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  LIT["{ id: 1, name: 'Ada' }"] --> OBJ[New object]
  OBJ --> OWN[Own properties\nid, name]
  OBJ --> PROTO[[Prototype]]\nObject.prototype
  OWN --> DESC[Descriptors\nwritable enumerable configurable]

snippet.label: Literals, shorthand, and computed keys
snippet.explanation: Line 1–2: variables used as shorthand keys. Line 7: computed property name built at runtime. Line 8–10: method shorthand — still a function property. Line 14: `this.id` works because `user.greet()` uses implicit `this` binding.

snippet.label: Reading and changing descriptors
snippet.explanation: Line 4: inspect descriptor flags. Line 7–11: redefine with stricter flags — requires `configurable: true` on the original to change later. Line 13: assignment fails when `writable: false`. Line 14: non-enumerable keys are omitted from `Object.keys`.

snippet.label: Symbol keys — unique and non-colliding
snippet.explanation: Line 1–2: each `Symbol()` is unique even with the same description. Line 5–6: symbol keys store data without polluting string-key enumeration. Line 11: `Object.keys` skips symbols; use `getOwnPropertySymbols` to find them.

blocks.title: Objects versus C# types
rows: C#: `new()` or object initializer; TS: type erased to plain object
C#: access modifiers in CLR metadata; TS: erased
C#: no direct equivalent; use typed wrapper
TS: yes at compile time; C#: nominal — must declare relationship

blocks.title: Assuming Object.freeze is deep
blocks.body: `Object.freeze(obj)` freezes only the top level. Nested objects remain mutable unless you freeze recursively. C# immutable records copy by value at the type level — different guarantee.

blocks.title: Using for...in without hasOwnProperty
blocks.body: `for...in` walks enumerable keys on the prototype chain too. Use `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` or `Object.keys(obj)` when you only want own properties.

blocks.text: At the engine level, a plain object is an **ordinary object** with internal slots: `[[Prototype]]`, `[[Extensible]]`, and a property storage model (fast elements vs dictionary mode). Literal syntax is syntactic sugar for `OrdinaryObjectCreate` plus `CreateDataProperty` calls. **Enumerable false** is how libraries hide implementation details from serialization — `JSON.stringify` only serializes own enumerable string-key properties. **Configurable false** prevents deletion and blocks redefining the property — used by built-ins like `length` on arrays. In production, confusing **own** vs **inherited** properties causes bugs when patching prototypes or mixing `Object.assign` with class instances.

blocks.title: Descriptor tradeoffs
rows: Assuming const makes nested fields immutable
Hidden symbol keys still exist — not secret, just omitted from enumeration
Once false, property is locked down permanently

snippet.label: Failure mode — mutating a frozen config in production
snippet.explanation: Line 1: top-level freeze does not recurse. Line 4: nested object still mutable — classic production footgun. Line 5: top-level assignment blocked. Strong answer: deep-freeze or immutable update patterns (spread copy).

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying `const obj = {}` makes all properties immutable — only the binding is const. Claiming Symbol properties are private — they are hidden from normal enumeration but readable if you have the symbol reference. Confusing `Object.keys` with all properties — it skips non-enumerable and symbol keys.

interviewTakeaways: Object literals create own properties with default descriptors: writable, enumerable, configurable all true.
Property descriptors control assignability, enumeration, and redefinition — not the same as TypeScript access modifiers.
Symbol keys are unique and omitted from Object.keys; they are not encryption or true privacy.

60s: Literals build plain objects with own properties. Descriptors are writable/enumerable/configurable flags. Methods are function properties — this binding is separate. Symbols avoid key collisions. Object.freeze is shallow. for-in walks the prototype chain unless you filter with hasOwn.
Follow-up: explain why JSON.stringify omits a non-enumerable property.
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'Object.freeze makes the whole tree immutable.' Strong: freeze is shallow; nested objects stay mutable unless deep-frozen or copied immutably.
Using for...in on objects without checking hasOwn — inherits enumerable prototype keys like toString in edge cases.
Treating Symbol keys as private — any code holding the symbol reference can read and write the property.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript checks object literal shapes at compile time; at runtime they are plain objects with no type name.
C# object initializers create typed CLR instances; JS literals have no nominal type at runtime.
